comments.rawMarkdown:
My take is that a ground-up RL or ML model by itself isn't going to be enough for ARC-AGI 3 because these games require prior knowledge about things like gravity/physics, cause-and-effect, and familiar representations like 'buttons', 'switches', etc. Plus, it requires the skill of planning ahead, and adapting as dynamics/rules change or compound. An RL model doesn't just learn this high-level thought process without an entirely different method of training and model architecture. I don't think generating more games to train on unlocks this higher level thought process.

World models (like [Dreamer v4](https://danijar.com/project/dreamer4/)) have shown promising planning ability, but they're planning over **known dynamics and environments** with clear reward signals. With ARC, figuring out the dynamics and rules **is** the task. You have to discover through exploration and then form an 'understanding' of the game in some persistent way.

Vision-enabled LLM's have already shown great results in solving levels of ARC-AGI 3, but the T4 VRAM constraints of the kaggle competition limit the 'intelligence' of the open source models that can be used.

comments.rawMarkdown:
I think an approach of generating lots of training examples would be necessary to complete this. The leading result in ARC-AGI-2, NVARC, won as a result of having a hundred thousand training examples that were generated mostly synthetically from mashups of public puzzles. I think porting existing puzzle games (someone has already done The Witness, i am looking at hard and varied sokobanlikes like Baba is You or Squishcraft) is probably the first necessary step.

From the NVARC approach, a large number(~2k) of non-synthetic examples are needed. This could be gotten from existing games, or from a game jam targeted at novel games compatible with the ARC-AGI-3 game engine. This would probably be better further into the competition as how well the current leaderboard does on your game would be a big indicator(negatively correlated of course) of how useful the game is.

Many puzzle games(take sudoku for example) can be generated in P time but take NP time to solve, so I do not believe that just being able to generate an arbitrary number of good-quality games would be enough to have a system perform well on another game, especially so since ARC has said that the private/test set games are out-of-distribution with respect to the public games.

One problem I can see is that the game in ARC-3 are very low resolution pixel art and also strictly one step at a time.
Should we manually convert games into this format? Or should we train on all resolution types and try to generalise at all resolutions? 
If we try and downsize most puzzle games, it can lead to artifacts and anti-aliasing issues. 
But... it still might give useful training data. 

A program to create synthetic games would be useful, but I think impossible to create by human hands! But it would be a fun challenge. Perhaps an LLM could write some code to create many games.

replies.rawMarkdown:
I think that using python `arcengine` library is already the best for that, as it would automatically be compatible with any architecture that can play the current public games. Given that no patterns should appear between the games, any DSL would presumably also be turing complete and so just using python would give a pretraining advantage.

One element of the game jam idea that I think would increase its effectiveness is having part of the scoring/ranking be how well/poorly the current leaderboard models do on the game. This would require participation between many teams, but I think it would be quite useful since the types of games not yet solveable by SOTA models would be highlighted.

comments.rawMarkdown:
My thinking is that an AGI model would have the capacity to operate at the level of domain-agnostic information, so like raw strings of real or binary values. At the highest level of abstraction, detecting patterns in any substrate is equivalent to finding a compressed representation of the information in that substrate (see algorithmic information theory). One might then be tempted to create training data by finding all compressions for strings up to some arbitrary length, and then training a transformer on those strings so it learns "general pattern recognition". The problem with this is that "finding all compressions" is actually incomputable, so you'd have to approximate it by working from specific models like CFGs, Markov models, combinations of sinusoidal functions, etc. 

But that might work? Just generate tons of synthetic "patterned" strings in this universal language of information by randomly generating various kinds of string generators and whatnot and use that to train a transformer. Then for a task like the ARC-3 it might be able to tease out order from chaos by compressing the stream of raw temporal data. Probably not efficient enough tbh, like others have said this challenge likely assumes too much prior knowledge - it's easy for humans because we have implicit knowledge of the various mechanisms already, it's not all sussed out from scratch during the game.

firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
If we are to use the standard neural network approach to this task, then we would need to generate lots of training data.

One method might be to get lots of old computer games (e.g. Atari) and put it in the right format for training.

Another method which I want to talk about is generating novel games. This seems extremely hard to do! To generate genuinely interesting games automatically, would not only give you valuable training data for this puzzle, but you could essentially repackage it as a mobile app as "Infinite fun games" to play. And make a gazillion dollars.

So this gives at least 2 motivations for creating software to generate interesting puzzles. 

First question:

* Would an app capable of generating interesting games also necessarily be advanced enought to solved them? Or can we separate the two?

Let's assume that we can create the puzzles, perhaps by starting from a solution and jumbling it backwards. This would not always create a puzzle that is humanly possible to solve. (e.g. imagine jumbling up a rubix cube - it is notoriously easier to jumble than it is to solve). 

Then we have the question of how to assemble both a set of rules/game mechanics and suitable starting and end states. One might try to compose different things like mazes, key/door, transporter, gravity, snakes, buttons, etc. But not all compositions would make for interesting games. Or one could imagine a more emergent system where simple rules might generate emergent mechanics without having them specified. (A maze might grow like a tree from a seed). 

Another problem is that our generated puzzles may not intersect with the type of puzzles in this competition.

I think only a machine trained on hours of youtube videos of puzzles and games will have any hope of solving the puzzles at human-level. And such a neural network will not fit into the memory allowed.

Packaging the puzzles into nxn coloured grids gives us the false impression that mechanical calculation is enough to solve the puzzles whereas indeed we need the sum-of-total-human-knowledge in order to solve them.

What's your thoughts on this matter?
